clue.text: Characteristic of radioactive decay found in lithium and iron

blocks.note: the straight definition: a physics term for how quickly a radioactive substance decays
the surface pushes a property of two metals; the setter means their chemical symbols, Li and Fe, written side by side, which make up half of the answer

explanation.surface: A line from a physics textbook about what happens inside two metals.
explanation.walkthrough: The chemical symbols Li and Fe join to spell LIFE, and that is only half the answer, so the phrase 'found in lithium and iron' is itself a half-life.
explanation.definitionFit: In physics the term names the time a radioactive sample takes to lose half its atoms, the standard measure of how fast it decays.

clue.text: Expect much fancied favourite to lose every time

indicators.note: every T (time) is lost from the joined words

blocks.note: HOT = much fancied, as a hot favourite, with its T removed
PET = favourite, with its T removed

explanation.surface: A punter doubting that the odds-on favourite will ever win a race.
explanation.walkthrough: T is the standard abbreviation for time, so 'lose every time' strips both Ts from HOT PET. 'Much fancied favourite' looks like one racing phrase but splits into two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To hope for something is to look forward to it as likely, close enough to expect.

clue.text: My choice of central elements in building

indicators.note: the choice is placed among the central letters
takes the middle letters of the next word

blocks.note: the two middle letters of buiLDing
OR is the word that offers a choice, placed between L and D

explanation.surface: Someone picking the core features of a building project they favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' opens the clue looking like a possessive, and it is the exclamation 'My!', the same as 'Lord!'.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Lord!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise.

clue.text: Pay off overdue £1 charges

indicators.note: to charge is to fill or load, so LATE is filled with I QUID

blocks.note: overdue = late
£1 = one quid, a quid being British slang for a pound; I is the Roman one

explanation.surface: A late-payment penalty of a pound on an overdue bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' reads as fees, which suits the billing surface, but it means 'fills': LATE is loaded with I QUID.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to liquidate a debt is to settle it completely.

clue.text: Study following nomadic Africans engages British polymath

indicators.note: 'following' means coming after, so CON is placed after the other letters
nomads wander, so the letters of AFRICANS wander into a new order
the rearranged letters take B into them

blocks.note: AFRICANS rearranged
B = British, slipped in after FRANCIS
to con is to study or pore over

explanation.surface: A scholar researching nomadic African peoples who takes on a British expert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British polymath' looks like one description, but British is B and only 'polymath' defines. Francis Bacon was the Elizabethan philosopher, statesman and scientist.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon wrote on law, science, philosophy and literature, the model of an English polymath.

clue.text: Have a go at wife leaving festive occasion

indicators.note: someone leaving departs, so W departs from the word

blocks.note: a wassail is a festive drinking celebration
W = wife, removed from the front

explanation.surface: A husband having a row with his wife as she walks out of a party.
explanation.walkthrough: Wassail is an old English Christmas custom of drinking and carolling.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'have a go at' is the informal phrase for attacking someone, physically or in words.

clue.text: Part of Egypt in Asia not entirely developed

indicators.note: ASIA loses its last letter
the letters are worked into a new form

blocks.note: the word itself
ASIA without its final A

explanation.surface: A geography note about a patch of Egypt that sits in Asia and is still largely undeveloped.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is true: the Sinai peninsula is the part of Egypt that lies in Asia, which makes 'in' look like part of the description rather than fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Sinai peninsula is the one region of Egypt lying east of Suez, in Asia.

clue.text: Criticise an author’s publicity material

blocks.note: the word itself
the author is the setter, 'I'; author's = I'M, I am
an advert is publicity material

explanation.surface: A reviewer slating the blurb a writer's publisher put out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Author's' reads as possessive, but it is 'the author is', the setter speaking of himself: I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: To animadvert on something is to pass critical comment on it.

clue.text: Ideal ground secures backing for facilities

indicators.note: ground as in ground up, so the letters are broken and remixed
backing is moving backwards, so MOORS goes into reverse

blocks.note: IDEAL rearranged
secures = MOORS (as a boat), run backwards

explanation.surface: A perfect site that lands financial support for new amenities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ideal ground' reads as a perfect plot of land, and 'backing' as funding; both are instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladies' room is a women's toilet, and facilities is a euphemism for toilets.

clue.text: Water to some extent absorbs toxic compound

indicators.note: PART takes AQUA into itself

blocks.note: in part = to some extent
aqua is Latin for water

explanation.surface: A warning that a toxic compound gets partly soaked up by water.
explanation.walkthrough: Paraquat is a highly poisonous weedkiller.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraquat is a herbicide that is dangerously toxic to people.

clue.text: Inane urban type lacking in consideration

indicators.note: inane means empty, so URBAN is emptied of its insides

blocks.note: URBAN with its middle removed leaves U…N
type = kind

explanation.surface: A sneer at a brainless city dweller with no thought for others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inane urban type' reads as one insult, a silly townie. 'Inane' is split off to mean empty.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: cruelty or thoughtlessness toward others is a lack of consideration.

clue.text: Staff in broadcast said to welcome argument

indicators.note: 'in' places a thing inside another, so MEN sits inside the word
the letters of SAID are scattered
to welcome a guest is to take them in, so GREET takes MEN inside

blocks.note: SAID rearranged
to greet is to welcome
staff = workers, men, placed inside GREET

explanation.surface: Employees on a radio programme are said to welcome a debate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast said' looks like news reporting and 'welcome argument' like a host inviting debate; 'Staff' means workers, not a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a quarrel between people is a failure to agree.

clue.text: Understand the difference record margin had in cuts

indicators.note: IN cuts into the string, landing between RIM and ATE

blocks.note: a disc is a record
rim = margin, edge
had (a meal) = ate
the word itself, cutting in before ATE

explanation.surface: A tally of how much a vinyl record's profit margin shrank after cutbacks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In cuts' reads as 'during reductions', but 'in' is the letters IN and 'cuts' tells them to break into DISC RIM ATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To discriminate between things is to perceive the difference between them.

clue.text: Revolutionary movement transfers power round

blocks.note: to hand something over is to transfer it
P = power, in physics
a ring is something round

explanation.surface: A political uprising that hands power to others all round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary movement' reads as politics; it is literal, a gymnastic move in which the body revolves over the hands.
explanation.definitionFit: A handspring is a flip in which the body turns a full revolution over the hands.

clue.text: Each point somebody thought fit to publicise?

blocks.note: every point of the compass: North, East, West, South
a somebody is a person of note, a worthy

explanation.surface: An editor asking whether each point a VIP made was fit to print.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Somebody' reads as 'someone', but it is the noun meaning a notable person: a worthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Something newsworthy is judged interesting enough to report publicly.

clue.text: Where Roman contests were seen some time back

indicators.note: the letters run backwards

blocks.note: an era = some time, a period

explanation.surface: A history note about where gladiatorial games took place long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some time back' reads as 'long ago', which fits the Roman surface; 'back' is instead the reversal of AN ERA.
explanation.definitionFit: Gladiatorial and other contests in Rome were staged in an arena.

clue.text: Celebrity to change course half-heartedly and begin again

indicators.note: the heart of VEER is its two Es; half of it goes

blocks.note: a star is a celebrity
the word itself
VEER = change course, losing one of its two central Es

explanation.surface: A famous person who loses heart in a new direction and resets.
explanation.walkthrough: Half-heartedly removes half of the heart, not all of it: VEER's middle is EE, and one E goes.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the phrase means going back to the beginning and trying afresh.

clue.text: Remarkable stable state that is difficult to achieve

definitions.note: the definition is a relative clause describing a noun

blocks.note: tall as in a tall story, hard to believe
order = a settled, stable condition

explanation.surface: A calm, steady condition that's hard to reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable state' could suggest a horse's quarters; it is simply order.
explanation.definitionFit: A tall order is a demand that is hard to meet.

clue.text: Ruin dreadful couple’s adopted son

indicators.note: adopting a child takes it into the family, so DIRE takes S into itself

blocks.note: dire = dreadful
S = son, placed inside DIRE
a pair is a couple

explanation.surface: A terrible couple whose adopted son wrecks everything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Couple's adopted son' reads as a family story; the son goes into DIRE rather than joining PAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Disrepair is a state of ruin through neglect.

clue.text: Ancient ship on lake moving slowly

blocks.note: L = lake, on maps
the Argo was Jason's ship in Greek myth

explanation.surface: An old vessel drifting slowly across a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down-reading instruction 'on' would mean above, but in an across clue ARGO simply follows L.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is a musical direction for a very slow tempo.

clue.text: In favour of member warning about introduction

blocks.note: pro = for
a limb is a member
an omen is a warning sign
on = about, concerning

explanation.surface: A committee member backing a caution about the opening remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: A prolegomenon is a scholarly preface; the rare word builds cleanly from four short pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A prolegomenon is an introductory essay to a learned work.

clue.text: Host seems clever eliminating every other part

indicators.note: every second letter is removed, leaving the rest

blocks.note: sEeMsClEvEr: the letters left after dropping every other one

explanation.surface: A presenter who looks sharp by cutting every second segment.
explanation.walkthrough: An emcee is an MC, a master of ceremonies.
explanation.definitionFit: An emcee hosts a show or event.

clue.text: Key passage in recital

indicators.note: a recital is spoken or performed, so the word is heard

blocks.note: an aisle is a passage between seats

explanation.surface: A crucial section in a piano recital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Key passage' reads as music; a key is a small low island, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: A key, or cay, is a small island.

clue.text: The buck stops here!

blocks.note: the surface pushes responsibility, as in 'passing the buck'; the setter means a male deer or rabbit
the surface pushes Truman's desk motto about final responsibility; the setter means the spot where the animal's body ends, its tail

explanation.surface: The motto of someone who accepts final responsibility.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase means taking ultimate responsibility; read literally, a buck is a male deer, and its scut is the short tail where the animal ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A deer's or rabbit's short tail is its scut, the point where a buck literally stops.

clue.text: Complete part of joint activity

indicators.note: the answer is a part of the following words

blocks.note: joINT ACTivity

explanation.surface: Finishing one share of a team project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complete' opens the clue looking like a verb, as in finish a task, but it is the adjective meaning whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Intact means whole, complete, undamaged.

clue.text: Line, say, reflected poem as written

indicators.note: a reflection turns EG round

blocks.note: say = EG, for example, turned round
an ode is a poem
sic, Latin 'thus', marks a quotation reproduced as written

explanation.surface: A verse line that mirrors itself and should be quoted exactly as printed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line, say' looks like a definition by example, but 'say' is EG; 'Line' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A geodesic is the shortest line between two points on a curved surface.

clue.text: Bloke on the radio that vents periodically

definitions.note: the definition is a relative clause describing a noun

indicators.note: radio carries only sound, so what comes 'on the radio' is heard, not read

blocks.note: geezer is British slang for a man, a bloke

explanation.surface: A radio presenter who periodically lets off steam on air.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words sound alike in British speech, where geyser rhymes with geezer.
explanation.definitionFit: A geyser is a hot spring that erupts at intervals.

clue.text: Most strict testers finish off examination with a twist

indicators.note: to finish off is to supply the end, so the last letter of the word is taken
the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
the last letter of examinatioN

explanation.surface: The toughest examiners end their exam with a surprise question.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is fully in the examination hall, which makes 'with a twist' read as a trick question rather than an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Stern means severe and exacting, so the superlative is 'most strict'.
